concept.name: CoDel (Controlled Delay) & Sojourn-Time Load Shedding
concept.title: CoDel (Controlled Delay) & Sojourn-Time Load Shedding
concept.tagline: Measuring queue sojourn time instead of static queue depth so goodput stays at 100% under overload.
concept.purpose: Understand why static FIFO queue-depth limits fail when downstream latency fluctuates, and how CoDel's sojourn-time target + LIFO/head-drop cadence prevents metastable goodput collapse.

prerequisites.title: Little's Law & Queueing Delay
prerequisites.summary: Know `L = lambda * W`: a queue of 1,000 items takes 100 ms when draining at 10,000 req/s, but 10 seconds when downstream slows to 100 req/s.

prerequisites.title: Monotonic Clocks
prerequisites.summary: Understand why `enqueue_ts` and `dequeue_ts` must use a monotonic clock (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) rather than wall-clock time.

spark.summary: CoDel tracks how long requests actually wait in a queue (sojourn time) over a sliding 100 ms window and drops head-of-queue expired items at a 1/sqrt(n) cadence when minimum sojourn exceeds a 5 ms target.
spark.keyTakeaway: When static queue-depth limits allow stale requests to pile up during downstream slowdowns, replace depth caps with CoDel sojourn-time load shedding so workers never waste CPU on already-timed-out requests.
spark.byteSummary:
A fixed `max_queue_size = 1000` works fine when downstream services run at 10,000 req/s (100 ms max wait), but the moment a database slows to 200 req/s, those 1,000 queued items take 5 full seconds to drain. Every client times out at 1 second, retries, and workers burn 100% CPU processing dead requests—collapsing goodput to zero.

CoDel (Controlled Delay), invented by Nichols & Jacobson for network bufferbloat and adopted by Meta/Envoy for RPC queues, ignores queue length and measures **sojourn time** (`dequeue_ts - enqueue_ts`) on every item. A healthy queue drains down to near-zero wait at least once per `interval` (typically 100 ms); a standing queue never drops below `target` (typically 5 ms) for an entire 100 ms window.

Once `min_sojourn > target` for a full `interval`, CoDel enters dropping mode: it drops the stale item at the head of the queue (or sheds incoming tail traffic in RPC proxies) and schedules the next drop at `interval / sqrt(drop_count)`. Because it acts on real time-in-queue rather than arbitrary item counts, CoDel needs zero manual tuning when downstream capacity changes.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & Why Static Queue Depth Collapses Goodput
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Exposes why `max_queue_size` cannot adapt when service throughput drops.

explanation.foundation: Suppose your service has a 1,000-slot FIFO queue and a 500 ms client timeout. Normally it processes 5,000 req/s, so a full queue drains in 200 ms.
explanation.core: Now a slow database query drops throughput to 500 req/s. A full 1,000-slot queue now takes 2,000 ms to drain! Every single request sits in the queue for 2 seconds, times out on the client after 500 ms, and gets retried—yet workers still execute all 1,000 dead requests, dropping useful goodput to 0%.
explanation.deepDive: Tail-drop (`reject new requests when len == 1000`) makes this worse: it keeps the oldest, already-expired requests at the head of the FIFO queue while rejecting fresh requests that still have time to succeed!

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: Sojourn Time, Target & Interval
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Defines the two parameterless invariants (`target = 5 ms`, `interval = 100 ms`) that separate bursts from standing overload.

explanation.foundation: CoDel attaches a monotonic `enqueue_ts` to every queued request. On dequeue, it computes `sojourn = now - enqueue_ts`.
explanation.core: A short traffic burst might push `sojourn` to 30 ms for 20 ms, then drain back to 0 ms—that's healthy buffering, so CoDel does NOT drop! Only if `sojourn` stays above `target` (5 ms) continuously for an entire `interval` (100 ms) does CoDel classify the queue as a standing bottleneck.
explanation.deepDive: Why `target = 5 ms` and `interval = 100 ms`? `interval` is roughly one human/RPC RTT window so transient bursts finish naturally, while `target = 5%` of `interval` ensures queueing delay never dominates tail latency.

sectionDiagram.title: Enqueue Timestamp -> Dequeue Sojourn Check -> Drop or Serve

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: 1 / sqrt(N) Drop Cadence & Head-Drop
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains why CoDel drops at `interval / sqrt(drop_count)` and why head-drop beats tail-drop.

explanation.foundation: Once CoDel enters dropping mode, it shouldn't drop every single request at once (which would cause wild oscillation), nor drop too slowly.
explanation.core: CoDel schedules the next drop at `next_drop = now + interval / sqrt(drop_count)`. Drop #1 waits 100 ms, Drop #2 waits 70.7 ms, Drop #4 waits 50 ms, smoothly ramping shedding rate to match the overload slope until `sojourn < target`.
explanation.deepDive: Dropping from the **head** (or using LIFO for overload) immediately evicts the stalest request that is already closest to client timeout, letting fresher requests behind it reach workers before their deadlines expire.

codeExample.title: CoDel Queue Dequeue Controller (Monotonic Clock)
codeExample.code:
import math, time

class CoDelQueue:
    def __init__(self, target_ms=5.0, interval_ms=100.0):
        self.target = target_ms / 1000.0
        self.interval = interval_ms / 1000.0
        self.dropping = False
        self.first_above_time = 0.0
        self.drop_next = 0.0
        self.count = 0

    def should_drop_on_dequeue(self, enqueue_ts: float) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        sojourn = now - enqueue_ts
        if sojourn < self.target:
            self.first_above_time = 0.0
            self.dropping = False
            return False
        if self.first_above_time == 0.0:
            self.first_above_time = now + self.interval
            return False
        if not self.dropping and now >= self.first_above_time:
            self.dropping = True
            self.count = 1
            self.drop_next = now + self.interval / math.sqrt(self.count)
            return True
        if self.dropping and now >= self.drop_next:
            self.count += 1
            self.drop_next = now + self.interval / math.sqrt(self.count)
            return True
        return False

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: FQ-CoDel & Tenant Isolation
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents one noisy tenant from triggering CoDel drops for well-behaved tenants.

explanation.foundation: If all tenants share a single CoDel queue, one tenant flooding 100K RPS pushes sojourn time above 5 ms and causes CoDel to drop innocent tenants' requests.
explanation.core: FQ-CoDel (Fair Queueing + CoDel) hashes requests by `tenant_id` (or priority class) into separate virtual queues scheduled via Deficit Round-Robin (DRR), running CoDel independently per queue.
explanation.deepDive: In RPC systems like Meta's `wangle`/Thrift, pairing CoDel with per-priority queues ensures `P2/P3` background work sheds immediately while `P0` checkout traffic stays untouched.

decisionFramework.problem: How to shed overload without tuning brittle queue-depth constants or hurting innocent tenants.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single shared FIFO queue with a fixed `max_size = 1000`.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Fixed depth cannot adapt when downstream throughput drops, and a single queue lets one noisy tenant starve everyone.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Static FIFO tail-drop vs. Single CoDel vs. FQ-CoDel (per-tenant/priority Deficit Round-Robin + CoDel).
decisionFramework.decision: Use CoDel sojourn-time shedding paired with per-tenant/priority queues (FQ-CoDel) and explicit `503 + Retry-After` responses.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Requires slightly more memory for per-tenant/priority buckets in exchange for automatic adaptation and noisy-neighbor isolation.

sectionDiagram.title: Tenant Hash -> Per-Tenant CoDel Queues -> DRR Scheduler -> Workers

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use CoDel
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents misuse on batch jobs or non-idempotent writes without client retry discipline.

explanation.foundation: CoDel assumes requests are short-lived RPCs where waiting in a queue longer than `target` (5 ms) signals overload.
explanation.core: When NOT to use CoDel: (1) Long-running offline batch/ETL queues (e.g., Spark/Celery jobs meant to wait minutes in a backlog) should use backpressure or autoscaling, not 5 ms CoDel drops; (2) If clients immediately retry `503` without exponential backoff + jitter, shedding only shifts load to retry parsing.
explanation.deepDive: Assumptions & Limitations: Default `target=5 ms, interval=100 ms` assume sub-50 ms microservice RPCs; slower LLM or analytics endpoints must scale `target` to ~5–10% of their baseline p50 service time. Glossary: Sojourn Time (`dequeue_ts - enqueue_ts`), Goodput (requests completed before client deadline), FQ-CoDel (Fair Queueing + CoDel).

decisionExercise.prompt: A background video-transcoding job queue intentionally buffers jobs for 2–5 minutes during traffic spikes. An engineer enables default CoDel (`target = 5 ms, interval = 100 ms`) on that queue. What happens?

options.label: Every queued job exceeds 5 ms sojourn time, triggering continuous CoDel drops and wiping out valid batch jobs.
options.explanation: Correct! Default 5 ms CoDel is for low-latency RPC queues, not asynchronous batch queues designed to absorb multi-minute backlogs.

options.label: CoDel speeds up video transcoding by 10x.
options.explanation: CoDel sheds queued items; it does not accelerate CPU work.

options.label: CoDel switches the queue to FIFO tail-drop automatically.
options.explanation: CoDel runs its sojourn loop as configured.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does CoDel measure queue sojourn time (`dequeue_ts - enqueue_ts`) instead of queue item count?

options.text: Queue item count cannot tell whether downstream throughput slowed down, whereas sojourn time directly tracks real waiting delay.
options.feedback: Correct! By Little's Law, 1,000 items can mean 50 ms or 5,000 ms depending on drain rate.

options.text: Counting items in a queue is O(N) in Python.
options.feedback: Queue length is O(1); the issue is semantic, not algorithmic.

options.text: Sojourn time eliminates the need for timestamps.
options.feedback: Sojourn time specifically relies on monotonic enqueue/dequeue timestamps.

options.text: Queue depth is always zero in distributed systems.
options.feedback: Queues build up whenever arrival rate exceeds service rate.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Sojourn time automatically adapts to changing downstream capacity without re-tuning static depth thresholds.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does CoDel wait a full `interval` (e.g., 100 ms) of `sojourn > target` before dropping any requests?

options.text: To distinguish short, harmless traffic bursts that drain naturally from a persistent standing queue.
options.feedback: Correct! A brief micro-burst should be buffered, not dropped.

options.text: Because TCP takes 100 ms to compute `sqrt(N)`.
To guarantee all clients time out first.
options.feedback: CoDel drops specifically to prevent client timeouts.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Waiting one interval avoids false-positive drops on temporary bursts.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does dropping from the HEAD of a standing FIFO queue improve goodput compared to tail-drop?

options.text: The head item has been waiting longest and is most likely already expired on the client, whereas tail items are fresh.
options.feedback: Correct! Evicting expired head items lets workers spend CPU on fresh requests that can still succeed.

options.text: Tail-drop is impossible on a linked list.
options.feedback: Tail-drop is trivial (just reject on push), it's just suboptimal under standing queues.
Head-drop discards stale items, not payload bytes.

options.text: Head-drop guarantees zero retries from clients.
options.feedback: Clients may still retry; returning 503 + Retry-After controls retries.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Processing expired head requests wastes 100% of worker CPU on work the client already abandoned.

beginner.summary: CoDel prevents queues from filling with expired requests by measuring how long items actually wait in line rather than counting how many items are queued.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When a queue slows down and requests start timing out, drop the oldest waiting requests based on wait time so fresh requests finish fast.
beginner.byteSummary: Counting queue items breaks whenever your database slows down. CoDel checks how many milliseconds each request waited and drops stale head items once wait time stays above 5 ms for 100 ms.

intermediate.summary: CoDel tracks monotonic sojourn time against a 5 ms target over a 100 ms window, shedding stale head requests at 1/sqrt(N) cadence.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When static queue limits cause goodput collapse under overload, use CoDel sojourn shedding with per-tenant FQ-CoDel queues.
intermediate.byteSummary: By tracking `dequeue_ts - enqueue_ts` over 100 ms intervals and ramping drops at `interval / sqrt(N)`, CoDel absorbs short bursts while shedding standing overload automatically.

advanced.summary: Per-tenant FQ-CoDel with monotonic sojourn tracking, 1/sqrt(N) head-drop cadence, and target scaling for high-latency RPC tiers.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When isolating noisy neighbors under standing overload, combine DRR per-tenant queues with CoDel sojourn shedding and backoff-aware 503 headers.
advanced.byteSummary: FQ-CoDel pairs Deficit Round-Robin tenant isolation with parameterless sojourn control (`target=5ms, interval=100ms`), preventing metastable retry collapse while protecting healthy tenants.
